title: Daley v. Aetna Life & Casualty Company
lead: An employee repeatedly seeks flexible scheduling and criticizes her employer’s public family-friendly claims. After discharge amid an existing performance-discipline history, she pursues speech, public-policy, misrepresentation, and other theories.

actors.name: Virginia Daley
actors.role: Aetna designer challenging discharge and related workplace conduct.

actors.name: Aetna Life & Casualty Company
actors.role: Employer defending scheduling and termination decisions.

actors.name: Michele Flynn
actors.role: Supervisor accused of retaliation, interference, and defamatory statements.

actors.name: Ronald Compton
actors.role: Aetna chairperson who received Daley’s critical memorandum.

proceedings: The trial court directed verdicts on three theories, and the jury found for defendants on remaining claims.
The Connecticut Supreme Court unanimously affirmed all counts, including derivative failure of the husband’s consortium claim.
limits: This transforms the canonical historical brief without a fresh audit or present employment-law certification. Employment facts follow what the jury reasonably could find. The repeated detailed February 10, 1993 termination date and November 1992 memorandum chronology control over conflicting introductory or assigned dates. Private-workplace statutory speech coverage and agent-interference availability were assumed, not decided.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Daley’s responsibilities expand amid performance concerns
paragraphs: Aetna hired Virginia Daley in October 1985 as an interior designer for home-office renovation. She moved to corporate leasing in 1989 and coordinated field-office design nationwide. On the evidence the jury reasonably could credit, her 1989 and 1990 reviews criticized communication, deadlines, unfinished assignments, and responsibility.

Michele Flynn became her supervisor in late 1990 during preparations for reduced design staffing. After learning Daley was pregnant, Flynn approved a $2,100 raise despite continuing concerns. Daley gave birth in July 1991, then took six weeks of paid maternity leave and two weeks of paid vacation.

sections.title: Flexible-work requests and discipline develop before the memorandum
sections.cue: What did Daley tell the chairperson?
paragraphs: Daley requested one work-at-home day each week on return. After consultation, Flynn denied it because reorganization increased workload, reduced staff, and required training, teamwork, and customer response. Daley considered that first refusal reasonable. Returning in September, she retained work while eight designers were laid off and received promotion to design project manager. Later flexible-schedule and weekly-vacation requests were also denied.

By early 1992 Flynn met with her weekly about deficiencies. A March warning began progressive discipline, and October brought probation. On November 9, Aetna’s internal paper announced a family-policy award to chairperson Ronald Compton. A week later, Daley wrote him criticizing the gap between promoted flexibility and her experience, referring to five unnamed coworkers’ failed requests, two departures, and need for greater implementation authority.

In December, improvement led Flynn to end probation, warning that recurrence within a year could mean discharge. By February 1993, deadlines and coordination again failed; Daley described three projects as on schedule despite missing materials orders and updates. Aetna discharged her February 10 for longstanding deficiencies.

sections.title: Trial resolves several theories by judge and the rest by jury
sections.cue: What did the public-policy exception require?
paragraphs: Daley sued Aetna and Flynn on multiple theories, and her husband asserted derivative consortium loss. The trial judge directed verdicts on public-policy wrongful discharge, interference, and negligent employment practices under a safety statute. The jury rejected the remaining claims. Daley appealed those rulings, evidence and instructions, speech treatment, and a defamation interrogatory; the Connecticut Supreme Court took the transferred appeal.

Justice Katz applied Sheets’s narrow wrongful-discharge exception: an improper discharge reason had to violate important public policy. Statutes, constitutional provisions, and judicially recognized policies could supply it, but courts should not casually replace management discretion. Even taking evidence favorably to Daley, no reasonable jury could find the proposed legal mandate here.

Family autonomy, leave and restoration statutes, pregnancy protections, women’s employment interests, and child-reporting law expressed important policies without requiring a weekly home-work arrangement. Daley conceded she was not treated this way simply for having a child, that denial was not necessarily unlawful, and that Aetna generally met Connecticut leave rules. Nothing extended child-reporting duties to her scheduling demand. Rejection of this expansion did not excuse pregnancy discrimination or existing leave violations.

sections.title: The speech claim turns partly on disputed context and motivation
sections.cue: Why was the memorandum not protected as a matter of law?
paragraphs: Section 31-51q prohibited discipline for specified constitutional rights. The court assumed without deciding coverage of private-workplace speech and addressed federal standards only because Daley claimed no broader state protection. Public-concern classification was legal, but disputed content, form, context, and motive could require factual resolution.

Whether her memo was broader citizen criticism or a personal schedule grievance was disputed. Interest to working parents did not settle that issue. Instructions properly distinguished personal complaints from public concerns without requiring speech to contain no personal element. A prior pleading ruling that allegations could describe generalized criticism did not predetermine the evidence-stage question.

Two redacted sentences described coworkers and calculated a seventeen-percent success rate. Though offered for motive and context, relevance depended on unsubstantiated circumstances or risked distracting disputes about departures during layoffs. Other text conveyed broader concern, and no harmful effect from redaction was shown. The speech verdict and evidentiary ruling stood.

sections.title: The remaining verdicts and directed rulings withstand review
sections.cue: What limits did each theory encounter?
paragraphs: Negligent misrepresentation required false information, not necessarily a contractual promise. Instructions about Aetna’s commitment and support were adequate in context: Daley knew arrangements depended on supervisory discretion and business needs and admitted they were not presented as entitlements. She identified no assurance that persistent pursuit could never lead to discipline; saying the company was less committed than advertised did not establish reversible instructional error.

The defamation charge separately read nine challenged performance statements, while the interrogatory collectively asked whether Flynn’s remarks stated fact rather than opinion. Trial courts had discretion over form. An adverse verdict alone did not prove confusion, and Daley had not challenged the charge’s adequacy. The court did not declare every workplace accusation immune opinion.

For interference, the court assumed an agent could potentially interfere with her principal’s employment relationship, but required improper motive or means and intentional unjustified interference, not mere ill will. Discipline predated the memo, performance problems were longstanding, and denials and instructions could be justified management. Daley’s own concessions reinforced insufficient retaliation evidence.
Section 31-49 concerned physical welfare and safety. Allegedly negligent management and discipline, without physically hazardous conditions, did not establish the general employment remedy asserted.

sections.title: All judgments remain for the employer and supervisor
sections.cue: Which questions were not resolved by the affirmance?
paragraphs: On August 3, 1999, the court unanimously affirmed every count. Chief Justice Callahan and Justices Norcott, Palmer, and Peters concurred with Katz, without separate writings. The husband’s consortium claim failed derivatively.

The ruling did not create a comprehensive rule for every future family-accommodation claim, determine broader Connecticut speech protection, decide private-workplace coverage reserved under § 31-51q, or resolve the assumed availability of an agent-interference theory. It sustained the actual verdicts and evidentiary and legal rulings on this record.
